heuristics.rule: 200+ applications is the baseline for international CS job seekers in the US
heuristics.condition: When an international student is applying for CS jobs in the US on OPT
heuristics.action: Target a minimum of 200 company applications, with 100+ referrals attempted; treat anything under that as insufficient effort, not bad luck
heuristics.because: The author states they applied to 200+ companies and got 4-5 offers; H-1B sponsorship restricts the pool significantly, so volume is required to compensate for the smaller eligible employer set

heuristics.rule: Start LeetCode preparation before school starts, not after
heuristics.condition: When an international CS student is planning their job search timeline
heuristics.action: Begin LeetCode from May (before August enrollment), aiming to have 500+ problems solved at least twice before fall recruiting season opens in September
heuristics.because: Fall recruiting (September) begins immediately after enrollment; students who wait until school starts lose the preparation window entirely

heuristics.rule: Prioritize fall recruiting over spring recruiting
heuristics.condition: When an international CS student is deciding when to focus their job search
heuristics.action: Treat the September–December recruiting window as primary; spring recruiting has significantly fewer open positions
heuristics.because: The author explicitly states spring recruiting has 'far fewer slots' and advises securing offers in the fall season

heuristics.rule: Deprioritize GPA once job search begins
heuristics.condition: When a CS student is in their final year and must allocate time between coursework and job preparation
heuristics.action: Choose easy courses, minimize academic effort, and redirect time to LeetCode and projects; GPA is not asked about post-graduation
heuristics.because: The author states 'nobody asks your GPA after graduation, they ask where you work' — signaling employers weight technical skills over academic performance

heuristics.rule: Tailor your resume to the specific role being applied to
heuristics.condition: When submitting applications — especially for roles that differ from some of your past experience
heuristics.action: Remove irrelevant experience and only include items directly relevant to the target role's requirements
heuristics.because: ATS (applicant tracking systems) at large companies auto-filter resumes; even highly qualified candidates get screened out for including unrelated experience

heuristics.rule: STEM OPT extension makes CS the dominant viable path for international students who want to stay in the US
heuristics.condition: When advising an international student on which field to pursue if US work authorization is a priority
heuristics.action: Strongly favor CS or other STEM fields that qualify for the 3-year OPT extension over non-STEM fields with only 1-year OPT
heuristics.because: 3 years of OPT gives 3 lottery cycles for H-1B versus 1 cycle for non-STEM — dramatically increasing the probability of obtaining work authorization

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines how many H-1B lottery attempts a student gets; 1 year = 1 attempt, 3 years = up to 3 attempts, fundamentally changing the probability of staying in the US long-term
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether your degree program qualifies for STEM OPT extension via the DHS STEM designated degree program list

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Sponsoring H-1B costs the employer money and creates administrative overhead; many employers exclude international candidates outright, shrinking the viable applicant pool
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check historical H-1B sponsorship records (available via USCIS public data / tools like myvisajobs.com); prioritize tech companies with established sponsorship pipelines

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Industries where domestic labor is abundant (finance, architecture, many science fields) have little incentive to sponsor international workers; tech is an exception because of demonstrated domestic talent scarcity
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research the ratio of international workers in the target industry and whether top employers have active H-1B sponsorship histories

decision_factors.factor: LeetCode problem volume and quality before recruiting season
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Technical interview performance is directly correlated with preparation depth; candidates with under 200 problems solved are described as statistically likely to fail at top companies
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count problems solved, assess whether you can independently solve medium/hard problems, and review past interview questions (面经) to test yourself

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Full-time roles at major companies are predominantly filled via return offers from internships; candidates without relevant internship experience face a much harder path to full-time roles
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess whether you have at least one CS-relevant internship before applying for new grad full-time roles; if not, prioritize internship applications first

decision_factors.factor: English verbal communication ability in interviews
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Interviewers assess social/communication skills alongside technical ability; poor interview English can cause a technically qualified candidate to be perceived as low on 'culture fit' or 'professionalism'
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Self-evaluate through mock interviews in English; identify if nervousness or limited vocabulary is causing performance gaps versus actual competence

decision_factors.why_it_matters: 1-year master's programs leave very little time between enrollment and the peak fall recruiting season, often resulting in students missing the prime internship cycle entirely
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Map your program's graduation date against recruiting cycles; 1-year students may need to start preparation before arriving on campus

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a non-STEM or non-CS graduate program in the US
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: 1-year OPT window provides only one H-1B lottery attempt; failure means mandatory departure with no fallback option, effectively making long-term US residency a near-lottery outcome
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who chose programs based on academic interest or rankings without understanding the OPT/H-1B pipeline implications

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Investing heavily in academic performance (GPA) over job preparation during the master's program
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Employers in CS do not ask for GPA post-graduation; the time cost of chasing high grades directly competes with LeetCode preparation and networking — the actual gatekeepers for employment
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who transferred their domestic academic mindset (GPA = success) to a US job market where technical interview performance matters far more

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Listing all experience on a resume without role-specific tailoring
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: ATS systems auto-reject candidates with irrelevant experience; a highly qualified candidate with a bloated resume may receive zero interviews despite strong credentials
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students from multidisciplinary backgrounds or those who pivoted fields (e.g., non-CS undergrad to CS master's) who try to show breadth

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on survival stories of international students in non-CS fields as evidence that your field is viable
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Survivorship bias: the vast majority who couldn't find work simply returned to their home country and are invisible in online discourse — the visible commenters are the exceptions, not the rule
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students in non-CS, non-engineering fields who see scattered success stories and assume they are representative

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Focusing job search on return to home country as a fallback without preparing simultaneously
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Domestic recruiting cycles (especially China's fall/spring recruiting) have fixed windows; missing them while pursuing US opportunities leaves the student with no fallback offer either
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who treat domestic employment as a guaranteed safety net that can be activated at any time

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying to top-tier companies (Google, Meta, etc.) after only 1-2 months of LeetCode preparation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Optimism bias + underestimation of competition level; students compare their preparation to domestic peers, not to the actual pool of competing applicants at those companies
failure_patterns.consequence: Mass rejection across top companies, followed by online posts attributing failure to the market being 'too hard' rather than insufficient preparation
warning_signs: Fewer than 200-300 LeetCode problems solved before first applications
Targeting FAANG exclusively before securing any offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Submitting a generic resume without tailoring it to the specific job description
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students treat the resume as a comprehensive CV (academic mindset) rather than a targeted marketing document matched to ATS keyword requirements
failure_patterns.consequence: Zero interview callbacks despite genuine qualifications; the candidate attributes failure to market conditions rather than resume filtering
warning_signs: Resume includes research or coursework from a different field than the role being applied to
Same resume submitted to all companies without modification
Resume exceeds one page for a new graduate with a mix of unrelated experience

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying to fewer than 50 companies and concluding the job market is impossible
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: International students compare their application volumes to domestic peers, not accounting for the much smaller pool of H-1B-sponsoring employers they are actually eligible for
failure_patterns.consequence: Premature exit from the job search process, missed opportunities, and false generalization that the market is closed to international candidates
warning_signs: Only applying to well-known companies rather than the full universe of sponsoring employers

failure_patterns.pattern: Spending OPT year without accumulating H-1B lottery attempts or building a Canada/alternative fallback
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students assume one lottery win is inevitable and don't plan for the possibility of multiple failed attempts
failure_patterns.consequence: After the OPT window expires without H-1B approval, the student has no legal status to remain and no pre-arranged alternative — forced to return home
warning_signs: No awareness of employer-sponsored Canada transfer options (e.g., Microsoft Vancouver)
No plan for what happens if H-1B lottery fails in year 1 or year 2
Non-STEM students who only have one lottery attempt

failure_patterns.pattern: Using academic proxy metrics (GPA, course difficulty) as the primary measure of job-readiness
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students import the academic success model from domestic educational systems where grades were the primary outcome variable
failure_patterns.consequence: High GPA but poor LeetCode performance and thin project portfolio; fails technical screens while believing they are well-prepared
warning_signs: Student talks about GPA when asked about job preparation
Choosing hard courses over practical CS electives to look impressive
No side projects beyond required coursework

diagnostic_questions.question: How many LeetCode problems have you solved, and how many times have you reviewed them?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Actual technical interview readiness, independent of self-assessment; below 300 problems (once through) indicates high probability of failure at top companies
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If 500+ problems solved twice: move to mock interviews and system design preparation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If under 200 problems: delay applications to target companies until preparation threshold is met; apply to mid-tier companies first for interview practice

diagnostic_questions.question: How many companies have you applied to, and do you have a tracking system?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student's search volume is appropriate for the international candidate pool; under 100 applications in a full recruiting season indicates effort, not market conditions, as the bottleneck
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If 200+: analyze the funnel — where are candidates dropping out (application → screen → interview → offer)?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If under 50: volume is almost certainly the problem, not market conditions or qualifications

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your target role/industry have a demonstrated history of sponsoring H-1B visas?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student's target companies will even consider their application; applying to finance, law, architecture, or other domestic-labor-abundant fields dramatically shrinks the viable employer pool
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: proceed with standard strategy; verify specific companies' sponsorship history
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: reassess target industry or identify the rare sponsoring employers within that field before investing further effort

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your degree program STEM-designated, and do you qualify for the 3-year OPT extension?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: How many H-1B lottery attempts the student will get; this is the single biggest structural determinant of long-term US stay viability
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If STEM: 3 lottery attempts — viable path if employer sponsorship is secured
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If non-STEM: only 1 lottery attempt — need to either secure employer sponsorship before graduation or plan a realistic exit strategy

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you done any CS-relevant internships, or is your experience exclusively academic?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student has the industry experience signals that ATS and recruiters screen for; academic-only candidates face significantly higher rejection rates at the resume stage
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If internship experience: assess relevance and ensure it is prominently featured with quantified impact
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no internship: prioritize internship applications immediately; a return offer from internship is the primary path to new grad full-time roles at top companies

industry_realities.common_belief: STEM fields are all roughly equally good for staying in the US after graduation
industry_realities.actual_reality: STEM designation only matters for OPT extension; the more critical variable is whether US companies actually hire in your field. Life sciences, chemistry, physics, and ecology have poor hiring demand despite being STEM — the 3-year OPT window doesn't help if no employer is willing to sponsor
industry_realities.implication: Students should evaluate both OPT eligibility AND employer sponsorship demand in their target field before choosing a program

industry_realities.common_belief: Finance and business degrees from US universities are strong credentials for US employment
industry_realities.actual_reality: US finance and banking industries are saturated with domestic talent; employers have little incentive to pay for H-1B sponsorship when qualified citizens are available. Non-CS business fields are among the hardest for international students to find US employment in
industry_realities.implication: International students targeting finance should either pivot to quantitative/technology roles within finance (where CS skills matter) or plan to leverage the US degree for return to home market employment

industry_realities.common_belief: Working hard academically and getting a good GPA will translate into better job prospects
industry_realities.actual_reality: For CS roles in the US, GPA is rarely asked about or screened after the initial application. Technical interview performance (LeetCode), project portfolio, and internship experience are the actual gatekeeping criteria
industry_realities.implication: Time allocation should shift dramatically toward LeetCode preparation, project building, and networking — not GPA optimization

industry_realities.common_belief: If you can't find work in the US, returning to your home country is a straightforward fallback
industry_realities.actual_reality: Domestic recruiting cycles in China (and likely other countries) operate on fixed schedules. Missing the fall/spring recruiting windows while pursuing US opportunities can leave students with neither a US job nor a domestic offer
industry_realities.implication: Students should track home-country recruiting timelines in parallel with US search, and not treat domestic employment as an always-available fallback

industry_realities.common_belief: People who couldn't find jobs in the US are vocal about it online, so the failure rate is visible
industry_realities.actual_reality: Survivors are dramatically over-represented online. People who failed to find US employment and returned home largely disappear from these forums. The visible discourse is dominated by CS students who found work — creating a systematic survivorship bias about how achievable US employment is across all fields
industry_realities.implication: Don't use online success stories as calibration for your own field's difficulty; actively seek out data on the full cohort, not just the visible successes

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Apply to 20-50 well-known companies, wait for responses, conclude the market is closed if rejected
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treat 200+ applications as the baseline minimum; use referrals for 100+ of those; view sub-100 applications as a data point about effort, not market conditions
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: International candidates have a structurally smaller eligible employer pool due to sponsorship requirements; volume is the primary compensating mechanism

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Start preparing after arriving on campus; assume 1-2 months of LeetCode is sufficient for top-company applications
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Begin LeetCode 3-6 months before recruiting season opens (May for August enrollment); target 500+ problems reviewed twice before first top-company applications
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Fall recruiting begins in September; students who start in August have almost no preparation window, and showing up underprepared to top-company interviews is a waste of interview opportunities that may not recur

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to evaluate job search difficulty
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: 'The market is hard' — based on personal rejection experience and online posts from peers
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Separate market conditions from individual preparation gaps; most online complaints about CS job search difficulty come from under-prepared candidates, not from people who completed full preparation cycles
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Misdiagnosing the problem (market vs. preparation) leads to wrong solutions (waiting for market to improve vs. investing more in preparation)

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Use one comprehensive resume showing all experience, skills, and projects across all applications
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Tailor resume to each role's specific job description; remove irrelevant experience; assume ATS keyword filtering before human review
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A comprehensive resume that includes irrelevant experience will be auto-filtered by ATS before any human sees it, regardless of how strong the underlying candidate is

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Focus on getting the job first; assume H-1B will work out or that there's a solution when the time comes
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Map out the full OPT + H-1B lottery timeline before accepting offers; identify employers with Canada transfer options or CPT-based fallbacks; build a multi-scenario plan from day one
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who don't plan for H-1B lottery failure get blindsided at the end of their OPT window with no legal status and no fallback

community_misconceptions.misconception: If you go to a top US university, finding a job in the US is relatively straightforward
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Domestic applicants with elite degrees do have strong employment outcomes; international students conflate the prestige advantage with the visa sponsorship hurdle, which affects all international candidates equally regardless of school ranking
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: School prestige helps with resume screening and interview access, but does not exempt international students from H-1B sponsorship requirements, lottery odds, or the structural disadvantage of competing against domestic candidates for a smaller pool of sponsoring employers
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students from top schools who don't understand the H-1B pipeline may be blindsided when offers fall through or are unavailable due to sponsorship constraints, despite their strong academic credentials

community_misconceptions.misconception: All STEM degrees give you equal advantage in staying in the US
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The STEM OPT extension (3 years) is often discussed as the key advantage, and all STEM fields qualify for it — so people assume the playing field is level across STEM
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: STEM OPT extension only helps if employers in your field actually sponsor H-1B. Biology, chemistry, physics, and many other STEM fields have poor sponsorship rates because domestic talent is sufficient. CS/engineering are the exceptions, not the norm
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students choose STEM programs outside CS/engineering expecting a 3-year path to H-1B, then discover that no employers in their field will sponsor them — leaving them with 3 years of OPT but no job offers with sponsorship

community_misconceptions.misconception: CS job search in the US is primarily hard because of the market, not individual preparation
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Online forums are disproportionately populated by people who are struggling — creating a perception that failure is the norm. Survivorship bias also hides the people who succeeded through preparation
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The majority of CS job search failures among international students are attributable to under-preparation (insufficient LeetCode volume, weak resumes, inadequate networking) rather than market conditions. CS remains the most favorable field for international students in the US by a significant margin
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students who believe market conditions are the primary cause don't invest in the preparation that would actually change their outcomes; they wait for conditions to improve rather than improving their own competitiveness

community_misconceptions.misconception: You don't need to worry about domestic (home country) job applications until after you've exhausted US options
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Students prioritize the US opportunity and treat domestic employment as a guaranteed fallback with flexible timing
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Domestic recruiting cycles in China and other countries operate on fixed schedules with defined application windows (fall and spring recruiting). Missing these windows while pursuing US opportunities can result in being locked out of both markets simultaneously
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students who fail to find US employment in their final semester discover that domestic recruiting windows have already closed, leaving them with no offer from either market

real_case_outcomes.situation: International CS student applying for US jobs with under 200 LeetCode problems solved, targeting top companies (Google, Meta level) after 1-2 months of preparation
real_case_outcomes.decision: Proceeded to apply and interview without meeting the preparation threshold
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Near-universal rejection; student attributed failure to market difficulty rather than preparation gaps and posted online about how hard the job market is
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Preparation volume (500+ problems, multiple passes) is not aspirational — it is a threshold requirement for top-company interviews. Applying below threshold wastes interview opportunities and produces misleading data about market conditions

real_case_outcomes.situation: Highly qualified MIT graduate with strong internship experience applying for CS roles but submitting a resume with all experience (including unrelated fields) without tailoring
real_case_outcomes.decision: Submitted the same comprehensive resume to all companies
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Received no interview callbacks despite strong qualifications; the issue was identified only when peers reviewed the resume and found irrelevant experience causing ATS filtering
real_case_outcomes.lesson: ATS filtering happens before human review; a bloated resume with unrelated content will be auto-rejected regardless of underlying candidate quality. Tailor to each role

real_case_outcomes.situation: International CS student who failed H-1B lottery but worked at a major tech company (implicitly Microsoft) during OPT
real_case_outcomes.decision: Leveraged employer's existing Canada transfer program to relocate to Canadian office
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Continued employment without interruption; maintained career trajectory through employer-sponsored Canada pathway
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Large tech companies (Microsoft, Amazon, Google) have established pathways to transfer employees to Canada when H-1B lottery fails; this option should be researched and negotiated before OPT expires, not after

psychological_barriers.trigger: Students describe the job market as 'too hard' or 'impossible' after a small number of rejections (20-50 applications)
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Attribution error combined with ego protection: it feels less threatening to blame market conditions than to acknowledge insufficient preparation
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Posting on forums about market difficulty, seeking validation that conditions are impossible, stopping the job search prematurely
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Ask the student to report their actual preparation metrics (LeetCode count, application volume, referral attempts) before accepting their market diagnosis; reframe the question from 'is the market hard?' to 'have I met the preparation threshold for my target companies?'

psychological_barriers.trigger: International students in non-CS fields express confusion about why they can't find US employment despite strong academic credentials
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Credential transferability illusion: students assume the academic prestige and hard work that earned their degree will translate directly into employment value in a market that operates by different rules
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Focusing on GPA and academic reputation while neglecting the structural reality that their field does not have H-1B sponsorship demand
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Separate the academic value of the degree from the employment market reality; introduce the concept of employer sponsorship demand as a variable entirely independent of academic quality

psychological_barriers.trigger: Students delay applying to domestic (home country) jobs while pursuing US opportunities, treating domestic employment as an always-available fallback
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Sunk cost fallacy + optimism bias: having invested heavily in US education, students resist closing the door on US employment and overestimate their ability to activate domestic options on demand
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Missing domestic recruiting windows; arriving at end of OPT with no offer from either market; experiencing shock that domestic fallback is not available
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe dual-track job searching as risk management, not hedging or giving up on US aspirations; treat domestic application deadlines as hard constraints to be tracked in parallel, not sequential fallbacks

psychological_barriers.trigger: Students express paralysis about whether to 'waste time' on LeetCode preparation versus school coursework
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Identity conflict: students who self-identify as 'good students' resist deprioritizing academic performance, even when the evidence suggests coursework has near-zero job market return
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Over-investing in coursework, selecting hard courses to maintain identity as high-achiever, then entering recruiting season under-prepared for technical interviews
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Validate the academic identity while reframing what 'preparation' means in this context: 'You're not slacking — you're optimizing for the actual exam, which is the technical interview, not your GPA'

reframing_moves.original_framing: CS job search in the US is very hard / the market is terrible
reframing_moves.reframe: The question is not whether the market is hard — it's whether you have met the preparation threshold. Most people complaining about difficulty online have solved under 200 problems and applied to under 50 companies. CS is still the best-positioned field for international students by a wide margin.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts focus from an external, uncontrollable variable (market conditions) to internal, controllable variables (preparation depth, application volume); breaks the helplessness framing
reframing_moves.example_language: 'CS找工作再难，也是全美第一的最好找工作的专业，没有之一。说找工作难的，90%都是这样的人在这说，自己没怎么努力。'

reframing_moves.original_framing: I've applied to 20-30 companies and haven't gotten any interviews — is the market really this bad?
reframing_moves.reframe: 20-30 applications is not a sufficient sample size to diagnose market conditions for an international candidate. The baseline for meaningful signal is 200+ applications; anything below that is a measurement of effort, not market receptivity.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Replaces a market diagnosis (which produces helplessness) with an effort diagnosis (which produces a clear action: apply more); contextualizes the international student's situation against domestic baselines
reframing_moves.example_language: '北美投简历，少于200家都是没努力。我们在北美是外国人，你20家努力了？'

reframing_moves.original_framing: Should I focus on getting good grades or finding a job?
reframing_moves.reframe: GPA is not the gatekeeping variable for employment. The gatekeepers are LeetCode performance, project quality, and internship experience. Once you understand what the actual 'exam' is, the resource allocation question answers itself.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes the false trade-off framing by identifying which metric actually matters; students can deprioritize coursework without feeling like they're failing — they're just redirecting effort toward the correct evaluation criteria
reframing_moves.example_language: '毕业了没人问你GPA多少，都会问你去哪工作了，所以分清孰轻孰重。'

reframing_moves.original_framing: Other international students in non-CS fields have found jobs in the US, so it must be possible for me too
reframing_moves.reframe: The people you see online are survivors — the majority who didn't find work returned home and are invisible in these forums. You're seeing the 10% success cases and inferring a 50% success rate. CS students complain online because they stayed; other fields are quiet because those students left.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Directly names and corrects survivorship bias; reframes the 'evidence' the student is using as systematically misleading; encourages more realistic prior about field-specific difficulty
reframing_moves.example_language: '幸存者偏差，其他专业都直接回国了，说话的声音都没有。'
